title: The Only Health Insurance Stock You Can Own with Michael Ha | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 51
summary: Michael Ha argues that UnitedHealth’s coding exposure and fragmented acquisitions outweigh a simple repricing recovery, while Medicaid may remain difficult until 2027-2029. He favors Alignment’s care model and discusses PBM fee flexibility. Eisman adopts broad sector caution but expressly has not researched Alignment. Subsequent evidence is mixed: UNH segments recovered, Molina remained strained, and Alignment grew while cutting profit guidance. Eisman’s specific expectation that final Medicare Advantage rates would not improve was wrong. Longer Medicaid timing and Alignment’s five-year target remain open, and clinical/coding causality requires more than raw company comparisons.
assessment: Full transcript read. Strong focus on segment economics and policy mechanics, but the host political-rate forecast failed and broad caution underweighted the possibility of company-level recovery. Primary results support selective rather than universal conclusions; unverified coding and clinical comparisons remain unresolved.
speaker_map_notes: Michael Ha is the Baird analyst guest. Eisman supplies hypothetical explanations and explicitly adopts overall sector caution/integration critique. Investor repricing counterarguments are exploratory, and Alignment targets belong to Ha alone.
framework_points: Use CMS cohort data to test coding exposure, but control for population composition.
Separate insurance repricing from provider-service economics.
Rate-setting lags and selection can move medical costs faster than premiums.
Vertical ownership does not automatically establish operational integration.
Compare clinical outcomes on risk-adjusted populations and consistent denominators.
Map all PBM compensation channels before forecasting profit effects of regulation.
tools_and_charts: CMS risk-score cohorts and acquisition timing
Optum segment margins and recast comparisons
Medicare Advantage advance and final rate notices
Medicaid acuity, redeterminations and rate lags
Medical loss ratios and star ratings
PBM formulary, rebate and fee economics
transcript_cautions: No opening montage; introduction references prior Claimable and Cuban interviews.
Life-insurance advertisement at roughly 1110-1205 is excluded from analyst claims.
ASR repeatedly spells Optum as Optim or Optimum; names normalized.
Ha corrects 80 hours per week to per month.
Host adoption is strongest in closing, but ALHC remains the guest recommendation.
Final CMS policy changed after the interview; distinguish rejected proposed calibration from continuing coding controls.
Admissions and denial rates are not comparable without denominator and risk-mix controls.

evidence.title: Medicare Advantage Medical Loss Ratio
evidence.finding: MA and Part D contract-level MLR must be at least 85%; violations can require remittances to CMS, enrollment restrictions and termination. MLR is a regulatory patient-care measure, not simply GAAP gross or net profit; it is not a universal 15% net-margin cap.
